title: EART-H
text:
I, C. Ezra Stiles, peripatetic cartographer of the Golden Fountain on Kiliman, do here present to the reader a work that hath consumed the better part of my life and the whole of my wandering. I am, by vocation and by sacred duty, a mapper of the holy sites — those granite tablets, iron cubes, sandstone arches, and all the greater forms through which the power of RA doth flow into the world. It is the charge of my order to walk the breadth of EART-H, to find these sites, to record their aphorisms, and to fix their positions upon the map so that those who come after us may know where divine power dwelleth. This is no mere occupation. It is a calling that demandeth the whole of a person’s body and the whole of their mind, for the sites are scattered without regard for the convenience of travellers, placed as often at the bottom of a ravine or upon a wave-battered reef as in any place a sensible person might think to look.
Yet in the course of these long peregrinations I have come to understand that the map is not merely a record of where things are. It is a way of thinking about the world entire. For one cannot chart the position of a sacred site without understanding the mountain upon which it sits, and one cannot understand the mountain without knowing the forces that raised it from the deep. One cannot reckon the journey between two shrines without knowing the rivers that must be forded, the winds that drive the rains, the beasts that hunt the passes, and the settlements where a weary traveller may find sustenance and shelter. And so, by degrees and over many years, what began as a simple catalogue of holy places hath grown into something far more ambitious: an attempt to set down the whole of what I know about the world — its shape, its airs, its waters, its peoples, and the strange and marvellous forces that bind them all together.
I confess freely that such an enterprise is, in its grandeur, almost absurd. What right hath a single cartographer to speak of the origins of the world, of the movements of the moons, of the great currents of trade and migration that have shaped the lives of millions? The knowledge contained herein is of such bewildering variety — touching upon the shape of continents and the habits of insects, the mathematics of celestial orbits and the customs of fisher-folk, the logic of settlement and the mystery of birth — that no one mind can truly hold it all at once. It is as though one were asked to draw a map not merely of the land but of the wind itself, and of the thoughts of every creature that the wind doth touch. I have done my best, and I ask the reader’s patience with an old man who hath perhaps reached beyond his grasp.
What I can offer is the testimony of my own experience, for I have walked upon every continent save frozen Amazonia, and I have spoken with folk of every station and condition. I remember the morning I first beheld the great fundament of Centre, when the mists parted and the mountains rose before me like the spine of some sleeping titan, and I understood for the first time that the bones of EART-H were not laid down at random but with a terrible and deliberate art. I remember the night I lay upon the deck of a Tusquean merchant vessel and watched two moons cross paths in the sky, their mingled light turning the sea to a sheet of hammered copper, while the sailors muttered prayers and the rigging hummed with an energy that made the teeth ache. I have sat with the ice-bearded shepherds of Salmon and heard them reckon the rains by the colour of the evening clouds with an accuracy that would shame any scholar’s instruments. I have argued with the physicians of the Fingers over the nature of Confluence until dawn broke grey through the windows, and I have knelt before golden fountains whose aphorisms I can still recite from memory, though their meaning remaineth as opaque to me as it was the day I first read them aloud.
All of this — the mountains and the moonlight, the rains and the roads, the settlements that rise and the knowledge that fades — I have tried to gather into the pages that follow. I begin with what little is known of our world’s creation and the vanished entity that made it. I proceed to the substance of the land itself, then to the moons that govern our fortunes, the airs and weathers that clothe the world in its many garments, and the sacred sites that order the distribution of divine power. From there I descend to the particular: the rivers and capacities that determine where people may dwell, the growth of societies from wandering bands to settled cities, and the roads and sea-lanes that knit those cities together. I have attempted, though with the humility of one who knows his limitations, to render all of this upon a single map. And I conclude with what I have learned of the great mystery of Confluence, and a chronicle of events that is, I freely confess, still very much a work in progress — more a collection of fragments and travellers’ tales than a proper history, and one that I hope to improve upon considerably before my legs give out entirely.
Knowledge is a strange thing. It is at once the most solid and the most fleeting of possessions. A mountain may be mapped and its position fixed for all time, yet the understanding of why it stands where it does may shift with every generation of scholars. An aphorism carved in stone endureth longer than any kingdom, yet its meaning changeth with every soul who reads it. I have spent my life gathering facts — the position of a shrine, the depth of a river, the number of days’ march between two cities — and yet I find that the more facts I gather, the less certain I become of what they mean when taken together. The world is vaster than any book, and more subtle than any map. All I can do is set down what I have seen, as faithfully as my art and my memory allow, and trust that those who follow will see further.


The Secret Text
The EART-H project adopts a practice from a fantasy series that I enjoy. In that world reading is understood as a feminine art and it is the practice among men of means (who cannot read or write themselves) to have women read to them for pleasure and edification. All that patriarchy aside, what I like about the way it is represented in the story is that texts all have footnotes made by generations of female readers that offer extensive and learned commentary on the texts themselves. These footnotes are withheld from the oral presentation of the works and the men know nothing about them. The footnotes create an entire alternative way of experiencing the text and encompass debates on the origins, authenticity, and historical context of the main text. I adopt a version of this practice here with the main narrative of EART-H presented in the chapters and a hidden set of commentaries presented as footnotes at the bottom of each page. You can choose to read them or not as you see fit.
Everything you see here was generated in R based on publicly available data. I used Claude.ai extensively in the generation of code, especially html, but have tried to keep it away from the text as much as possible.
Enjoy, Christopher Stiles Fowler Great, great, great grandson of Ezra Stiles who revitalized the curriculum at Yale during his presidency in the 1770’s and corresponded extensively with Benjamin Franklin. His voice here is that of Sir John Mandeville, fictional author of Mandeville’s Travels (published circa 1357) whose attempt at scholarly rigor and utter credulity make the perfect voice for my ‘book’

title: 2  Origins
text:
2.1 In the Beginning…
Of all the chapters in this work, the one that follows is the most perilous, for it concerns matters that no living soul can claim to have witnessed. What I set down here is drawn from the oldest fragments of scripture, from the oral traditions of peoples who reckon their histories in song rather than ink, and from the speculations of scholars who have spent their lives sifting truth from legend. I have gathered these accounts as faithfully as my art allows, yet I must warn the reader that where the other chapters of this book rest upon the firm ground of observation — mountains I have climbed, rivers I have forded, cities whose markets I have walked through — this chapter floats upon the waters of conjecture, and the reader must judge for themselves how much weight it will bear.
Now it is to be known that, as far as the wisest clerks can reckon, the Univers[ity] was always in existence, having neither beginning nor end that any sage has yet discerned. Our story begins when the entity [Profes]Sor [Fow]Ler conceived of an idea most wondrous. And from that idea, and from the power granted unto Sor Ler, there were created hundreds of worlds, all of them different yet strangely similar one to another, as though fashioned by the same hand but with a different purpose in each fashioning.
EART-A and EART-B were the first to emerge from this great labour, and their stories are told elsewhere, for now. But EART-H, where our story takes place, was among the very first, and I say to you truly that the care of its design reveals the art of far more than a mere clockmaker. For Sor Ler appointed the entity called RA to oversee EART-H, and in the early days it is said by those who keep the oldest records that RA was ever present upon the land—building up the mountains with great force, filling the seas to their very brim, and shaping with patient craft the earliest creatures that did roam the world.
I have heard from many peoples in many lands the oral histories that have been passed down from generation unto generation, and they speak of late nights when the mottled face of RA could almost be perceived in the heavens, vast and terrible and full of purpose. Whether these stories be apocryphal or have, within them, a kernel of truth, none living can say with certainty. What is known, and upon this all the learned I have consulted do agree, is that centuries if not millennia have passed in which EART-H has not known direct action by RA.
And though some peoples do still burn offerings to this vanished entity, as I have witnessed with mine own eyes in the highland shrines and coastal temples alike, the world itself has moved on, playing out the magnificent experiment that this being orchestrated, with no understanding among any of its inhabitants of how or why it continues to run.

title: 2  Origins
text:
2.2 The Great Experiment
Now I shall speak of the great experiment itself, for its nature remains one of the chiefest mysteries of EART-H, and I have put the question to every wise one and learned clerk I have encountered in my travels. The scholars of many lands do hotly debate whether the complex interplay of the three moons was made intentional by design, whether the distribution of magical energy across the breadth of the planet serves some greater purpose yet hidden from mortal understanding, or whether EART-H has simply grown and changed beyond its creator’s original vision, as a garden left untended will put forth strange new shoots. But what is not in doubt among any who have eyes to see is that this is an experiment. For in my wanderings I have beheld with mine own eyes how the landscape is littered with dozens if not hundreds of idiosyncratic places and items that clearly have their origins elsewhere, being of a craft and substance not native to this world. Some of these places, like those that offer healing to the sick and the weary—and I have visited many such sites and felt their virtue upon my own person—are patterned with such regularity across the continents that some plan must assuredly be at work. Yet the nature of that plan remains opaque even to the most diligent of seekers. I have furthermore heard tell of numerous cults that have risen and fallen over the centuries, each purporting to predict the end of the experiment and thus the end of EART-H itself, but so far, praise be, the experiment continues at its own pace and with its own mysterious logic.

title: 2  Origins
text:
2.3 The Vanishing
I have consulted many ancient chronicles and spoken with keepers of the oldest libraries, and the historical records do suggest that RA’s presence upon EART-H began to wane approximately 2,000 years ago, though the exact reckoning of that timeline remains much disputed among the learned. The last confirmed manifestation of RA, so far as any trustworthy source can attest, occurred during what is now called the “Extension,” a most marvellous event in which several major magical artifacts were created simultaneously across different continents, as though the hand of the maker reached out in many directions at once before withdrawing forever. Now, while most processes upon EART-H seem to have proceeded without interruption since that time, I have journeyed to several parts of the planet where the living order of plants, beasts, and waters hath gone wild and strange in the absence of direct influence, like a horse that has thrown its rider and gallops where it will. These places draw both scholars and adventurers in great number, for their obvious flaws are thought to shed light upon the underlying logics of the experiment, and they do furthermore produce higher than average numbers of inexplicable phenomena—wonders and terrors alike that I have witnessed and shall recount in later chapters of this work.

title: 2  Origins
text:
2.4 Today
And now I shall tell you of EART-H as it stands in this present year of 2026, for I have seen much of it with mine own eyes and can speak with some authority. It is a complex and diverse world, marvellous in its variety, yet I say to you that it is characterized by chaos more than by order. The surges and ebbs of lunar power, governed by the three moons in their ceaseless dance, do make long-term projects most difficult to complete, and many a great work has been left unfinished when the tides of power turned against its makers. The societies of EART-H have adapted to this instability in various and cunning ways: some have embraced the nomadic life, carrying their households upon their backs and following the currents of power as a shepherd follows their flock; others have developed intricate systems of alliances and trade to mitigate the risks that attend such fluctuations. No one civilization holds dominion over the whole of the planet, and there remain vast reaches of land and sea that are but lightly settled, where a traveller may walk for days without meeting another soul. We cartographers, who seek the wisdom of the healing sites, have visited most corners of the world in our quest to unravel the order and disorder of that great system, yet I confess that many remote locations have seen fewer than a dozen visitors in centuries, and what marvels they contain remain unknown to all but the wind and the beasts.


This project has emerged from my desire to create a world in which I can explore ideas about power, identity, and social formation. I am increasingly intrigued by the literature on Futurisms, and the claim that emerges from that work that we have difficulty imagining just futures because we are so closely tied to the present and the institutions we already have in place. By creating a world with different rules; particularly related to property rights and racial identity, I hope to be able to explore these ideas in a way that is less bound by my own experiences.
Imagination is disciplined by what we take to be settled fact, so that the institutions we live inside come to feel like features of the world rather than decisions somebody made. Ursula Le Guin in her 2014 National Book Award speech says “We live in capitalism, its power seems inescapable — but then, so did the divine right of kings. Any human power can be resisted and changed by human beings” (Le Guin 2014). That sentence is more or less a guiding premise of this project and one that has been dear to me since I first read J.K. Gibson-Graham’s The End of Capitalism (As We Knew It) (Gibson-Graham 1996), which insists that the economy is not one totalising system but a field of practices we have simply learned to describe as one. Mark Fisher’s Capitalist Realism (Fisher 2009) is another version of the same; the argument that the horizon of the thinkable has closed, and that this closure presents itself to us as mere realism. Fisher opens by invoking the notable line that “it is easier to imagine the end of the world than the end of capitalism” — a sentence usually attributed to Fredric Jameson (though Jameson himself introduces the line with ‘someone once said…’ Jameson 2003). His Archaeologies of the Future (Jameson 2005) and others that I have been reading treat utopian writing as a diagnostic instrument; what we cannot imagine tells you what we take for granted (Muñoz 2009; Levitas 2013).
The Futurisms literature pushes this further, and they are the reason I am building a world rather than writing an essay about one. Kodwo Eshun (Eshun 2003) argues that the future is contested territory, already colonised by other people’s projections, so that imagining otherwise is a political act rather than a recreational one. Walidah Imarisha and adrienne maree brown (Imarisha and brown 2015) make the practical case that organising is science fiction — that anyone working toward a world which does not yet exist is already writing speculative fiction, whether or not they call it that. And Grace Dillon’s Walking the Clouds (Dillon 2012), which named Indigenous futurism, offers a concept I have found useful here: Biskaabiiyang, returning to ourselves — the idea that one cannot imagine forward until one has unlearned the frame one was handed. Arturo Escobar’s Designs for the Pluriverse (Escobar 2018) argues that design is ontological: in making a world we make the terms upon which it can be inhabited. That is what this is. I have changed two rules— what the incentives are for establishing private property and how the visible traits of identity are inherited— and the remainder of this book is an attempt to follow those two changes honestly wherever they lead.
Concurrently, I have become intrigued by the idea of storytelling as a way to teach students about geography and about the topics of population, economy, and institutions that I teach in my classes (Cameron 2012; M. Ortiz 2026; M. B. Ortiz et al., n.d.). I am increasingly aware of the limitations of lectures conducted in front of students who are only partially engaged. I worry about a world in which ideas are simply something that gets looked up or sourced from an AI instead of things that are chewed on, tested, and refined. My hope is that this project can serve as a starting point for a new way of teaching students–through stories and through play. My intent is to use these footnotes moving forward as a place to make connections between the academic literature that motivates both this project and the implementation here. Ultimately, I am not sure whether I am making a game, a book, or a syllabus. Perhaps all three.

title: 3  Physical Geography
text:
3.1 The Fundament
The most ancient legends and such fragments of legends as survive in crumbling scriptoria do affirm that the whole of EART-H’s landmass was wrought by RA in a brief and terrible season known among the learned as “The Funding.” In our present age this hath led scholars and sages of every province to speak broadly of the stuff whereof EART-H is made as ‘fundament.’ I have spoken with explorers who have noted, as their forebears noted before them these many centuries, that EART-H is composed of most cunningly structured systems of mountains, rivers, valleys, and streams – formations whose character of rock and shape of land may persist in like fashion for miles upon miles and then, of a sudden, change utterly. These places of change are held by some to be holy, for in their careful study we might come to apprehend something of RA’s great design for EART-H. Whether this be true or no is a matter upon which I, a mere cartographer, can only wonder – but in this chapter I shall set forth the story of creation as the most reliable scholars have pieced it together from their divers enquiries….

title: 3  Physical Geography
text:
3.2 In the beginning….
In the beginning – and this I have on the authority of the most venerable clerks and holy ones with whom I have taken counsel in my wanderings – there was naught but water. A great and featureless deep, stretching in every direction beyond the keenest eye’s reckoning. Whence this water came, or by what miracle the seas did not rise up and swallow all when vast continents appeared as if from nothing – these are mysteries that even the wisest sages bid me not to question. It simply was so, and so it remained.

It is by reason of this position, and the centrality it holdeth in the myth of RA, that the landmass is called Centre; and the folk who dwell therein, among its high ridges and deep-cleft valleys, do attribute unto their land a holiness that no traveller can fail to mark upon their arrival.

The peoples of this region depend upon that mighty watercourse for their very survival, and its fish – unusually robust and plentiful beyond all expectation – do sustain a far denser pattern of settlement than the high elevation and parched landscape would otherwise permit. title: 3  Physical Geography
text:
3.7 The final pieces fall
And now I come to the last and grandest act of RA’s labour, which the sages say came when their resources were nigh unto spent, or when some cosmic balance was at last achieved. For RA’s final contributions were two vast continents, each far greater in extent than any that had come before. First there appeared a massive polar land, ringed along its southern border by mountains so impossibly high that none I have spoken with claimeth to have seen their summits clear of cloud. Next – and almost as if RA had resolved at the very last moment that there must needs be more trees and more lakes upon the face of EART-H – a huge granite massif rose from the deep, covering much of the Northeastern quarter of the planet with its dark forests and shining waters.






Figure 3.14: The incredibly tall peaks of Amazonia could be glimpsed from miles and miles away, while Canada’s forests would ultimately come to be home for some of the largest population groups on EART-H.

title: 3  Physical Geography
text:
3.8 The World So Far
And so, as RA’s great work continued, the Fundament did take its shape, transforming from that endless and primordial ocean into a world of wondrous diversity – of mountains and valleys, of rivers and broad plains. With 80.45% of its surface yet covered by water, EART-H now possessed ten distinct continents, each bearing its own character and countenance, fashioned by divine intention and by those geological processes which the scholars of our age do continue to study and dispute amongst themselves. I, C. Ezra Stiles, have set foot upon every one of these lands, and I tell you truly: each is a world unto itself.

title: 3  Physical Geography
text:
3.9 The Shaping of the Margins
Yet the work of creation was not complete with the mere placement of land upon the waters. For where continents lay close upon one another, or where the deep sea met abruptly with high cliffs of stone, the fundament was rough and ill-joined, as a mason’s wall before the mortar is set. And so there came a further shaping – a gentling of the margins, as the learned scholars describe it – whereby the boundaries between land and sea were given their proper shelving, and the places where one fundament abutted another were knit together with more natural gradation. This was, perhaps, the final act of RA’s geological craft: the smoothing of seams, the laying of continental shelves beneath the shallows, and the ensuring that water, when it fell as rain upon the high places, might find its way downward to the sea without impediment.






Figure 3.15: The completed fundament of EART-H, with continental shelves shaped and the margins between lands smoothed by RA’s final geological craft.





My design for this section was drawn in part from the work of Ross Thorn whose presentation at NACIS circa 2018 gave me the idea for creating a fantasy landscape by twisting and altering real digital elevation data. Accessing the data is relatively easy it turns out, but not every place makes for a good continent. Then, once data is downloaded the real problems begin. Chief among these is dealing with movement of large landmasses across the dateline, and particularly in the polar regions.
One of the things I am most interested in is how these places appear when they are out of scale and facing very different climate conditions. Will an experience of the Finger Lakes be different when they are steep inlets to the sea? How will the region around the River of No Return Wilderness be experienced when it is placed up near the North Pole?
Why real terrain and not noise
The obvious way to build a fantasy world is to generate the terrain procedurally (e.g. rough shapes sketched, mountains and rivers by feel, then some fractal displacement to add detail and make it not look quite so clunky). I chose not to for several reasons. The first is mechanical; Real landmasses have real hydrology and reflect the geologic and hydrologic processes that have shaped them. The second has to do with the act of imagination that I want to bring to this project. When we take something real and familiar and make it into something completely different we begin the process of re-thinking what we know about that place. The continents here are mostly places near and dear to me (with a scattering of places that fit a need – looking at you Canada, Amazonia, and Kiliman). The act of imagination I want to invoke in myself and in the readers of this book is one that immediately takes the familiar and, literally, turns it on its head.
The cost is that I inherit the landscape’s real history whether I want it or not. By making this a story about RA placing continents and Stiles’ observation that junctures are places that shed light on RA’s plan I am trying to make a strength out of something that is actually a weakness– when Centre juts into Tusque and the junction produces breaks in hydrology, radical shifts in elevation, and general chaos it becomes the storyline rather than a failure of my method. Splendidly, this resonates with early work in geography by some of the greats. Hepach, quotes Livingstone (who I read in my 1st semester of grad school) who is writing about early work in geography saying that for early geographers (in this case Carl Ritter) “To study geography was to explore nothing less than the very laws of the Creator, who was the author of the human story, the architect of the world-plan, and the builder of humankind’s earthly home.”(Hepach 2023, 468; citing Livingstone 1992, 141).
I highly recommend Hepach’s work who sees similar views in the writings of Alexander von Humboldt (“the external world has no real existence for us beyond the image reflected within ourselves through the medium of the senses. As intelligence and forms of speech, thought and its verbal symbols, are united by secret and indissoluble links, so does the external world blend almost unconsciously to ourselves with our ideas and feelings. (Humboldt, 1849 [1845]:59, emphasis by author)”(Hepach 2023, 469)), and especially Carl Sauer.
Sauer’s The Morphology of Landscape (Sauer 1925), another 1st term reading in grad school and something I also read as an undergrad, is famously understood as the origin of cultural geography – the belief that we can understand place as the outcome of the intermixing of culture and natural area. Sauer is still revered by geographers today as an antidote to the racist environmental determinism that plagued the earliest instances of the discipline (but see Duncan’s critique, also used in grad school to teach me the meaning of ‘reification,’ Duncan 1980). That viewpoint is important here because the world I will describe in subsequent pages is initially deterministic down to the placement of roads and the size of settlements, but because this world is meant to be played, the tableau I set here is essentially the natural landscape with the cultural landscape still to be imagined. Simple, definitely reifying, but still open-ended to the human imagination. We leave terrestrial geography for a moment and fly to the moon(s).

title: 4  The Lunar System
text:
4.1 Lunar Intensity
The planet EART-H possesseth a most singular geography, shaped not by the labours of men alone but by the great tides of energy that pour forth from its three moons. These moons–Io, Ganymede, and Deos by name–do circle the world in orbits of marvellous complexity, ever turning and crossing one another’s paths, so that the surface of the earth is never long at rest from their influence. And I have seen with mine own eyes how, where their light doth strike the ground, it chargeth plants and beasts and even the very stones of the field with a magical energy of wondrous potency, which the inhabitants have learned to harness for all manner of purposes both great and small.

title: 4  The Lunar System
text:
4.2 The Three Moons
Now I shall speak particularly of each moon in its turn, for each doth emit a form of energy that careful practitioners–whom the wise ones of these lands call channellers–may bend to create the most astonishing effects. Yet these effects do wax and wane according to the nearness of each moon unto the surface of EART-H, and so the inhabitants have, by long study and observation, learned to track the moons with great diligence, as a mariner watcheth the stars.

4.2.1 Io - The Red Moon
Of the red moon Io I must speak first, for it is the most fearsome and changeful of the three. It followeth a path most steeply inclined against the plane of the world and moveth in retrograde–that is to say, against the natural turning of EART-H–so that it sweepeth across the heavens in a manner most dramatic, creating terrible variations in magical intensity from one latitude to the next. Many clerks and learned sages have told me that its energy is the energy of transformation and change, and I can well believe it, for I have seen its red light fall upon a quiet valley and set all things therein to strange and sudden alteration.


4.2.2 Ganymede - The Green Moon
The green moon Ganymede followeth a path of moderate inclination, and I have observed a most remarkable property of its magic: that it doth persist longer in inanimate objects than the enchantments of the other moons. Indeed, several species of plant have adapted themselves most cunningly to Ganymede’s pattern of movement, taking full advantage of the charge it bestoweth upon them to grow with great vigour during periods of peak exposure. This moon circleth the earth in a stately fashion, passing over the same point upon the surface roughly once in every seven days. For this reason the wise women do link Ganymede to growth, healing, and the natural magic that runneth through all green and living things.


4.2.3 Deos - The Blue Moon
Of the blue moon Deos I shall say that it possesseth the most stable orbit of the three and moveth most slowly across the firmament, so that it doth intersect more frequently with the light patterns of its sister moons. Its steadfastness maketh it the ideal instrument for calculating the passage of time, and for this reason the astrologers and seers of EART-H do associate it with time, memory, and the magic of divination–by which they seek to know what is hidden and what is yet to come.








Figure 4.2: Moon orbital paths over the past week

title: 4  The Lunar System
text:
4.3 Lunar Energy Distribution
Now it must be understood that the moons do possess dramatically different levels of power upon the surface, according to how far they stand from any given point at any given hour. For at any one time, a full half of the world lieth in darkness with respect to each moon’s light, and there may be places–as I have witnessed in my wanderings–where no moonlight falleth at all, so that the land is bereft of all celestial charge; and yet in other places, by the strange conjunctions of their orbits, the light of all three moons doth shine together with a power most formidable.








Figure 4.3: Lunar energy intensity across EART-H on 06 August 2026





I tell you in good faith that this variability in magical power, brought on by the ceaseless shifting and interplay of the three moonlights, is among the most crucial matters for understanding the evolution of all life upon EART-H. For I have spoken with naturalists and beast-keepers in many provinces, and they all do affirm that different species–and indeed different individuals within a species–possess an affinity for one type of moonlight above the others. This affinity may be trained and strengthened over the course of a lifetime, yet with rare exceptions, the one who groweth strong in one form of light doth thereby limit their capacity to work with another. And in certain rare cases, which I have heard told by trustworthy witnesses, individuals of especially powerful affinity for one form of light may be positively weakened and made infirm by exposure to the others.
At the most primal level of the natural world, the highly adapted species do bestir themselves when their favoured moonlight shineth strongest upon the land, and go dormant–sheltering in holes and dens and the deep places of the earth–when they are at their weakest. The natural world hath devised an almost infinite number of stratagems by which species have seized upon advantageous niches through the exploitation of these power differentials, and I have seen with mine own eyes how in certain places the visible flora and fauna do change utterly from one phase of the moon to the next, as though one had stepped from one country into another entirely.
What is true for the plants and beasts hath also shaped the development of the sentient peoples. In some provinces, power structures have arisen upon collaborative models, reflecting the wisdom of communities that must hedge their fortunes against periods of weakness in one form of moonlight or another. Other societies, by contrast, have found means to specialize, building institutions linked to particular types of power; yet these societies do favour mobility as their chief protection during seasons of weakness. And I must here record a most extraordinary marvel: in at least one case, a company of powerful sorcerers hath produced a flying castle–a great stronghold borne aloft upon enchantment–that moveth across the landscape directly beneath the blue moon Deos, so that their particular form of magic is always at its maximum potency, despite the very slow pathway that the moon doth travel across the surface. I have not seen this castle with mine own eyes, but many credible travellers have sworn to me upon their honour that it is so.
The mathematics of the lunar system are a major area of study upon EART-H, for practitioners do seek most earnestly to predict the timing and intensity of moonlight at specific locations. The complexity of the interactions maketh this a task of fearsome difficulty, yet over the passage of many ages a number of heuristics have been devised that do allow for reasonably accurate predictions. These predictions are of the utmost importance for the planning of agricultural cycles, magical rituals, and even the campaigns of war–for no general of sound mind would march their army into battle without first consulting the lunar tables.








Figure 4.4: Annual mean lunar energy intensity, sampled over one year







The power surges of the three moons are at the very heart of this project as it first took shape. I spend a lot of time in my classes thinking about how property rights shape the reality of our world. I have always wondered what the world would be like if it wasn’t so reliant on private property and the original idea for the moons was based on my wondering what it would take to make property rights a losing strategy for human settlement.
My thinking on this is drawn significantly from James Scott’s book Against the Grain (Scott 2017). In this book Scott argues that hunter gatherer societies were more resilient, had better nutrition, and spent less time laboring than agricultural societies in the early days of human plant cultivation. He argues that agriculture was not a priori superior to hunter-gatherer society, it was demonstrably worse, but that the hierarchy of the agricultural societies and the infrastructure of that hierarchy made them very effective at growth and better adapted to dealing with the needs of larger societies (especially the creation of institutions for managing internal conflict within larger and more complex socieities). Agriculture is not inevitable because it is better, it is inevitable because it expands better, keeps better records of its success, and gobbles up adjacent societies to function as labor in its production system.
A side note I want to explore later is the degree to which Scott’s compelling narrative is consistent with current views in Anthropology. Graeber and Wengrow’s The Dawn of Everything (Graeber and Wengrow 2021) is an example. They accept Scott’s demolition of agriculture-as-progress but reject any account in which hierarchy follows inevitably from grain, arguing instead that people cultivated casually for millennia without committing to it, and that some societies took up agriculture and then set it down again. The idea of theirs I find most useful here is seasonal dual morphology — societies that lived under a chief through one part of the year and dispersed into egalitarian bands in the next — a real ethnographic version of one of my imagined outcomes induced by the moons.
What is that imagination and how does it connect to moon energy? First, I am imagining species that adapt to moon cycles (more on this later in chapter 5), those species surge and wane creating irregular harvests that resist one of Scott’s preconditions for an agricultural hierarchy – predictable harvest size, time, and location. Second, moon energy on this planet conditions power and while one moon is dominant certain individuals will be strong, but those same individuals will be weak at other times when their moon is absent from the land. Control of land is ultimately about power, but if we cannot reliably guarantee the ability to control a particular piece of property, then why would we grow crops there? Someone could come along and simply take them at harvest time if it happens to fall at a moment when we are weak. The metaphor that strikes home for me here is the fact that strawberry plants need to be protected from chipmunks and rabbits at precisely the time of year when I am most busy. I only allocate the time to protect them one year in ten and so I almost never harvest berries. There is a particular chipmunk that rubs this in by leaving the partially eaten first berry of the year on my doorstep every May.
Anyway, in conditions of shifting power, property has to become more mobile I think. Settler colonialism begins in our own world when property rights forced the poorest to move elsewhere to find room to plant paired with the quest for power associated with the control of new lands by the already land rich. Perhaps in a society where control of land is less stable societies become more communal? In our world control of land generated wealth that was then available for use in trade. It returned rents that created generational wealth and long term inequalities that underpin almost every social injustice we have. What if land didn’t have this power? Would we have found other ways to create difference? This is one of the primary axes I want to explore in EART-H.
Anyway, what would it take for a world to hold off the development of property rights that stem, seemingly inevitably, from agricultural production as a dominant form of human organization? My answer? Highly variable power so that the warlord of one day would be an easy mark the next day. Interestingly, my original partners in imagining this world–notably including a sociologist/demographer–were highly skeptical that shifting power would be enough to disrupt property rights. I agree to the extent that I don’t think it would disrupt hierarchy, but whether that hierarchy would insist on property rights is, for me, an open question. A huge challenge of building this world is separating out the pieces that are truly deterministic (like the math for calculating moon orbits) and the pieces that only seem that way because it is what we are used to (back to LeGuinn and Jameson from chapter 1).

title: 5  Climate and Biomes
text:
5.1 Of the Climate of EART-H
RA, our maker, was no learned clerk of natural philosophy, yet they possessed a goodly and sufficient understanding of how heat and water, latitude and altitude, do conspire together to fashion the manifold living garments of the planet’s surface. From the frozen polar wastes, where the very breath of a traveller doth turn to crystals upon the wind, to the lush tropical forests, where the rains fall without ceasing and all manner of green and creeping things do flourish — this world supports a most remarkable variety of kingdoms of life, as I have witnessed with mine own eyes in my many journeyings.

title: 5  Climate and Biomes
section: 5.2 Of Temperature, Which Governeth All the Rest
text:
5.2 Of Temperature, Which Governeth All the Rest
Now I shall speak of Temperature, which is the very foundation and chief governor of all the climates of EART-H. For in my travels I have found it to be a most certain truth that the heat of the world doth vary in orderly fashion with latitude — being greatest and most fierce at the equator, where the sun standeth highest and burneth without mercy, and coldest at the poles, where winter holdeth perpetual dominion. Moreover, as one ascendeth into the high places and mountaintops, the air doth grow thin and the warmth diminisheth, so that even beneath a tropic sun one may find frost upon the peaks.





Global temperature distribution across EART-H

title: 5  Climate and Biomes
section: 5.3 Of Precipitation, and the Waters That Fall
text:
5.3 Of Precipitation, and the Waters That Fall
Of the Rains and Waters that fall upon EART-H, I must confess that their patterns are of a far more marvellous complexity than those of temperature alone. For the manner by which moisture is bestowed upon the land is governed by many intertwined causes — the latitude of the place, its nearness to the great oceans and seas, the prevailing winds which blow hither and thither across the globe, the shape and height of the mountains and valleys, and indeed the temperature itself, for warm air doth carry more water than cold, as any mariner will attest. The great rivers of wind that the learned call the Gales of Passage do sweep across the middle latitudes in broad meandering bands, carrying with them the storms and tempests that water the lands beneath their passage.





Annual precipitation patterns across EART-H




And so it is that these sundry forces, working in concert upon the airs and waters, do give rise to four great girdles of climate, which I have myself traversed; and I shall set down here not only what I have seen but also the causes that are alleged for them, leaving the reader to judge which are true and which are the invention of idle folk in winter.
About the belly of the world lieth the Girdle of Perpetual Rain, where the waters fall without ceasing and the air is grown so thick that a candle will scarce keep its flame. A monk of Tusque, one of great learning though much given to drink, did assure me that the sun standeth so near overhead in that place that it boileth the ocean as a pot upon a fire, and the steam thereof must needs come down again, there being nowhere else in all the world for it to go. Others hold that the equator is the very seam whereat RA joined the two halves of EART-H together, and that it leaketh. I have examined the ground most closely in three provinces and can confirm only that it is wet.
To either side of this girdle lie the Thirsty Lands, where a traveller may journey a twelvemonth and see no rain at all. The sages of those parts do reason that the water which riseth at the belly of the world, having gone up so exceeding high, overshooteth in its falling and cometh down elsewhere, as an arrow loosed too strongly flieth past the mark; which seemeth to me plausible enough. But the common folk say rather that these are the places where RA sat down to rest amid the labour of creation, and the ground was scorched by their sitting. And in truth the sand in certain parts is glassy, as though it had been burned, so I do not lightly dismiss them.
Further still lie the Temperate Girdles, which are the most agreeable to habitation, where the rains come in their season and the storms walk from west to east in orderly procession, like pilgrims who know the road. Here the learned are all in agreement as to the causes, which I take for a sign that they have not thought upon it very hard.
And at the two caps of the world lie the Frozen Wastes, where almost no rain nor snow falleth at all — a thing which astonished me greatly, for I had supposed the poles to be the wettest places of the earth, being the coldest. But it was explained to me by a whaler of the northern seas that cold air can carry but little water, as a beggar can carry but little gold; and that the snow which lieth upon the northern land is not new-fallen but ancient, having been in that place since the Funding, and merely blown about from spot to spot by the wind, so that it seemeth always to be snowing and never is. Whether this be so I cannot say.
Yet the two caps are not brothers, and this the maps do not tell you. At the northern cap there is land, hard and ancient and ringed about with mountains. At the southern cap there is no land at all — only a cold and landless sea, and at the very heart of that sea the water turneth. I have not seen it and do not intend to. Those few mariners who have come within sight of it and returned again speak of a whirlpool of such compass that one standing at its lip cannot see across to the other side, and they say the sea poureth down into it without ceasing and is never emptied, and that the sound of it may be heard a full day’s sail before ever the thing itself is seen.
What becometh of all that water, none could tell me. Some hold that it feedeth a serpent which lieth beneath the world and drinketh for ever. Others say that RA left the bottom of EART-H unfinished, having wearied of the labour, and that what we call a whirlpool is but the hole where the making stopped. And a cartographer of my own fellowship, who was drunk when they said it and sober when they would not repeat it, told me the sea goeth not down at all but goeth through, and cometh out again upon some further side; which I set down only because it is the manner of thing that soundeth foolish until one hath heard it twice.
I will add here, and let the reader make of it what they will, that in the deep interior of Amazonia there is said to be a river that runneth hot — hot enough to scald a hand, steaming in the cool of the morning, rising up out of the ground from no spring nor snowmelt that any traveller hath found. I have never been to that place. I have only ever heard it spoken of by those who had likewise never been. Whether such a river is, and whence its waters come, I leave to wiser heads than mine.

title: 5  Climate and Biomes
section: 5.4 Of the Biomes, or Kingdoms of Life
text:
5.4 Of the Biomes, or Kingdoms of Life
Now I shall tell of the Biomes, which are the great living provinces of EART-H, for it is a most wondrous thing that the marriage of temperature and precipitation doth beget eight distinct kingdoms of life upon the surface of this world. Each biome, as the learned do call them, representeth a unique and particular combination of climatic conditions — of heat and cold, of wetness and drought — which doth sustain its own peculiar assemblage of plants and beasts, as different one from another as the palm tree is from the pine, or the camel from the caribou.





Biome distribution across EART-H

Physical geography is not my strong suit and I ended up relying heavily on AI to select plausible parameters for each stage of this climate framework. The current version incorporates terrain-based orographic effects (using slope and aspect) and jet stream enhancement bands at approximately 30° and 60° latitude. I am still not entirely happy with the precipitation model, which remains more deterministic than I would like, but it is a significant improvement over the earlier version which suffered from a visible artifact where the continental outlines appeared shifted in the precipitation output.
The temperature model uses a latitude^1.5 relationship (steeper mid-latitude gradients than a quadratic), altitude-dependent lapse rates, and regional noise. The precipitation model layers latitude bands, jet stream enhancement, ocean proximity (multi-scale), terrain-based orographic effects, temperature-moisture coupling, elevation drying, and mesoscale noise. Biome thresholds include per-cell noise for more natural boundary transitions.
The technical pieces aside, this was a fascinating journey for me and I would like to develop the framework here into a five-week course on physical geography. What little I could contribute comes from my own undergraduate exposure in “Introduction to Physical Geography” and I would love to get one of my colleagues to help me build it out.
For the most part, my understanding is that the major elements of climate are complex, but ultimately deterministic. The planet needs to be in motion because everything in the universe is in motion. It needs to be in orbit because things that are not in orbit tend to crash into stars or black holes. If it is in orbit it has a relationship with a star and that star provides a source of light and heat. From there we get temperature. I have not specified tilt or elliptical orbit, so I don’t think there are seasons. The complexity of seasonal temperature variation will probably have to wait for the next version. I will have to keep that in mind as I write stories within the world. From temperature and supplied altitude I get temperature variation. Then we have precipitation, which of course assumes water. I tried for a long time to think of ways that straightforward temperature bands and even supply of water could be made more complex, but I am not entirely happy with the result. Biome ultimately arrived deterministically from temperature and precipitation and I had it in the back of my mind to try and match Earth’s own breakdown. It turns out that my efforts to pick exciting landscapes made for a lot more mountainous terrain and I really did throw in Canada at the last minute to make up for a deficit in temperate forest.
A hope of mine for this chapter is that is straightforward enough for students to modify and/or rebuild as they learn some physical geography. I am sure that I have missed some important elements (seasons!) and I would love to see how the information that follows is impacted by those elements.
If you are reading this and happen to have any expertise in climate science and or its implications for speculative fiction, I would welcome any pointers. A starting bibliography for now includes:

How to Find a Habitable Planet, James Kasting (Kasting 2010) — planetary habitability: what has to be true of a planet before anything can live on it.
Atmosphere, Weather and Climate, Roger Barry and Richard Chorley (Barry and Chorley 2009) — the standard climatology textbook
“Whirligig World”, Hal Clement (Clement 1953) — a 1953 essay describing how the planet Mesklin was built outward from its physics.
“The Creation of Imaginary Worlds: The World Builder’s Handbook and Pocket Companion”, Poul Anderson (Anderson 1974) — a working method for deriving a planet’s geography and climate from its star and orbit.
The Great Derangement, Amitav Ghosh (Ghosh 2016) — argues that the realist novel cannot represent climate, having been built to handle the probable, while climate arrives as the improbable; a case for the speculative register.
Sense of Place and Sense of Planet, Ursula K. Heise (Heise 2008) — on the difficulty of holding local attachment and planetary scale in mind at the same time.
Anthropocene Fictions, Adam Trexler (Trexler 2015) — survey of the climate change novel.
Science Fiction and Climate Change, Andrew Milner and J. R. Burgmann (Milner and Burgmann 2020) — sociological survey of climate science fiction.
Green Planets, Gerry Canavan and Kim Stanley Robinson, eds. (Canavan and Robinson 2014) — collection on ecology in science fiction.

title: 6  The Green Bounty
text:
6.1 Of the Plants and their Ways
Of all the marvels I have encountered in my wanderings, none hath proved more vexing to the understanding — nor more consequential to the daily lives of every soul upon EART-H — than the manner by which plants do grow, flower, and yield up their fruits. For the green things of this world are not as the green things of a simple garden, obedient to the turn of seasons and predictable in their harvest. Nay, they are creatures of the moons, as much as any beast that walketh or any sorcerer who channelleth, and their behaviour is governed by the same ceaseless flux of celestial energy that shapeth all else upon this world.
Here I must set down the thing I was slowest to learn, and which I beg the reader to hold in mind through all that follows. I was raised in Kiliman among people who till, and I grew up supposing, as a child will, that tilling was the thing people were for. The chronicles did nothing to correct me. They are written in the places that have grain, by those who eat it, and they leave a reader with the impression that a country is its fields. It is not so, and I had walked three continents before I understood how badly it is not so. The greater part of what is eaten upon EART-H was never planted by any hand. It springeth up of its own accord where the red light hath lately fallen, and is found, and followed, and gathered. The people who live so are not poor cousins to the farmers; they are the ordinary condition of this world. It is the settled farmer, bound to a field and reading it as a clerk readeth a ledger, who is the curiosity. I shall come to them in their turn, and I shall put them in their proper place, which is a small one.

title: 6  The Green Bounty
section: 6.2 Of the Three Natures of Plants, Concerning Which the Learned Do Not Agree
text:
6.2 Of the Three Natures of Plants, Concerning Which the Learned Do Not Agree
Through long observation, and much conversation with herbalists and naturalists, I have come to understand that the plants of EART-H may be divided broadly into three natures, according to which moon holdeth the greatest sway over their growing. The natures are not rigid, for many plants partake of two or all three; and the learned disagree most vigorously about the particulars. The herbalists of Stockholm insist there are not three natures but seven, whilst a scholar I met in the Fingers maintains that all plant behaviour proceeds from the working of moonlight upon a substance he calleth viridis humour, which he believes floweth through the roots as blood through veins.
I set down the simpler scheme, but I add a caution that every learned account I have read omits, and which anyone who has been hungry knows at once: the three natures are nothing like equal in the belly. Books give the greatest space to the grains, because grains are what books are written about. The stomach ranks them otherwise.

6.2.1 The Ganymede-Touched, or Bloom Plants
The plants that respond chiefly to the green moon Ganymede are the grains and the fruiting trees — the bread and the wine of EART-H, and the least of its larder. Let no one mistake me: the bloom is precious. It is what is eaten at weddings and hoarded against winter, and a people who lose their grain will grieve. But if every bloom field upon this world failed together in a single season, the peoples would tighten their belts and go on. Ganymede, as I have recorded in an earlier chapter, passeth over the same point roughly once in seven days, and the bloom plants store through the dark days and then erupt when the green light falleth. I was told by a naturalist of some repute that in the equatorial regions they grow so fast one can hear them, a faint crackling like parchment crumpled. I paid this man four coins to be taken out at night to hear it. I did hear something, and I am no longer certain it was the wheat.
But here is the crux of the matter, and the source of endless frustration for any who would seek to govern the harvest from afar: the bloom is not triggered by Ganymede alone. Beyond that much I can report nothing with confidence, for no two authorities will tell you the same thing, and each is contemptuous of the others. The farmers call the fortunate conjunctions by a hundred local names — the Quickening, the Green Tide, the Seven-Day Promise, the Breath of Ganymede — and each region hath its own tradition of reading the signs.
The grain farmers of Adirondaq hold that Io’s red light, arriving too soon before the green, doth suppress the bloom: the green moon proposeth, but the red moon disposeth. The herbalists of Stockholm say the flat opposite, that red light ripeneth and the fault lieth in having too little of it; they were angry with me for repeating the Adirondaq saying and would not take wine with me after. And an old woman near the coast of Banff told me the moons have nothing to do with it whatsoever, that a field bloometh when it hath been spoken to kindly and sleepeth when it hath not. She had forty years of good harvests behind her and I had none, and I record her opinion with the rest.
What I can say is only what I have seen: that the same field, under what appeared to my eye to be the same green light, will bring forth in one month and refuse in the next; and that on one slope near Banff the fields yielded three times in a season while those beyond a low ridge yielded once. The farmers there called it moonshade and were satisfied. I was not, but I had nothing better to offer them.


6.2.2 The Io-Touched, or Spreaders
Here is what the peoples of EART-H actually eat. The red moon Io is the moon of transformation, and the plants that answer to it are the most aggressive and opportunistic of all vegetation — the weeds, the pioneers, the colonisers of bare ground after fire or flood or the retreat of ice. They wait for nothing. They seize upon a surge of red light and grow with explosive speed, flinging seed and runner across any ground left open, and within days a hillside that was stone and ash is a thicket a man may lose himself in.
And the greater part of that thicket is food. Not fine food — the spreaders are coarse, and bitter until cooked, and a person raised upon them will tell you frankly that they would rather have bread. But they are everywhere, and they are enormous in quantity, and they come again within the month somewhere else. Nine parts in ten of what is eaten upon this world grew without anyone’s leave.
The spreaders are no gentle providence, mind. They take the bloom fields too if a harvest is left standing a week too long, and the most feared of them is the scarlet bindweed, which I have seen cover a stone wall in a single night with Io at its zenith, its tendrils glowing faintly red. There are stories in every province of settlements abandoned for a season and found overgrown to the rooftops. In the telling I had from a carter on the Tusque road the settlement was never abandoned, and the people were found still within their houses, grown over where they sat; but he was a carter, and it was late, and he had been paid in drink for two other stories already that evening. I have visited three places said to be that settlement and found at each a ruin of no great age with nothing on it but ordinary bramble.
To live upon the spreaders is therefore to move, and to move is the common life of EART-H. The gathering peoples follow the red surges as a mariner follows a wind, and a wise woman of the coastal marshes told me her people read the colour of the undergrowth as a sailor reads the sea, the bright red-green of new Io growth pointing toward food as surely as a needle points north. This is knowledge, and hard-won, but it is not knowledge of a place. It travels in the head of whoever holds it. A gatherer driven out of one country by war or famine is not ruined; she is merely somewhere else, reading a different hillside by the same signs. There is no lord in the world who has found a way to tax that.


6.2.3 The Deos-Touched, or Root Sleepers
The blue moon Deos is the moon of time and memory, and the plants that hearken most to its influence are the strangest and most patient of all. These are the root vegetables, the tubers, the great underground storehouses of energy that grow invisibly beneath the soil for months or even years before they ripen. The root sleepers, as the farmers call them, absorb blue moonlight slowly and steadily, building their reserves in darkness, and they do not reveal themselves until a particular alignment of all three moons triggers their maturation. Some natural philosophers believe that the root sleepers are not truly plants at all, but a form of earth-bound creature that hath learned to mimic plant life; I record this opinion without endorsing it, though I will say that I once saw a freshly dug root sleeper twitch in a manner most disconcerting, and that the labourer beside me did not look at it, and did not look at me, and went on digging. In the northern provinces they will tell you further that the root sleepers move — that a field dug over and found empty will yield in plenty three years after, the roots having come across from somewhere else beneath the ground. The natural philosophers of Tusque say this is nonsense and that the farmers merely dug in the wrong place, which may well be so. But I would observe that the farmers of the north are not in the habit of losing their own fields, and that a thing may be nonsense and true at once, as I have found more than once upon this journey.
Of all the crops of EART-H the root sleepers are the least governable, for the plain reason that nobody can see them. A tax collector may walk the length of a rich field and perceive only bare earth and common grass. There are tales of tubers the size of a grown person’s torso pulled from ground nobody had ever cultivated, and in the highlands of Salmon I was shown a grandmother root that took six labourers two days to lift, and which they swore had been swelling since before their settlement was founded.
But here I must correct an error I carried with me for a long while, and which I think most travellers carry. I had supposed that finding root sleepers was a village secret — that each community held the knowledge of its own ground and no other. It is not so. Finding them is a trade, and it is practised by people who go where they please. The root-finders read slope and water and the age of the ground, the manner of the grass above, the way the frost lies of a morning; and these signs, they insist, hold true from one end of a continent to the other. A finder trained in the Fingers may cross to Adirondaq and be at work within a fortnight. I asked several of them whether the ground of a strange country did not confound them, and got in every case the same faintly insulted answer: that a root is a root, and earth is earth, and only a fool learns one hillside when they might learn the principles.
This is why the root-finders are welcome everywhere and beholden nowhere. Their craft is their own, it walks out of the door with them, and a lord who hangs one has merely lost a finder. I asked an elder among my own people in Kiliman whether the singing that accompanies the work findeth the root or maketh it. I was told the question was foolish, and then given two different answers to it by two people who had each called it foolish.

title: 6  The Green Bounty
section: 6.3 Of the Bloom-Farmers, and Why There Are So Few of Them
text:
6.3 Of the Bloom-Farmers, and Why There Are So Few of Them
Now I come to the settled farmers, and I have kept them until last on purpose, for they are the strangest people upon EART-H and everyone mistakes them for the ordinary sort.
A bloom field cannot be read from general principles. It must be learned, one field at a time, over generations, and the learning does not carry. In the province of Centre, which I know better than most, the farming families keep almanacs written in a script devised for the purpose by a council of their forebears, so that a literate stranger sees only meaningless marks; I was shown one and could make nothing of it, though the woman holding it read it as I read these words. Elsewhere the same knowledge is kept in chants learned at the hearth, and I am told some communities divide it deliberately — the book holding the moonlight sequences, the songs holding which field is which — so that neither a stolen ledger nor a captured elder yields the whole.
Consider what this costs them. Such a family cannot leave. Their wealth is not in the grain but in four generations of knowing this particular slope, and that knowledge is worth nothing a valley away. They are the only people on this world who can be found in the same place twice, and they know it, and so does everyone else. Where lords have arisen upon EART-H — and they have arisen, here and there, and I shall speak of them in a later chapter — it is upon the backs of bloom-farmers, because there is nobody else to sit upon.
And yet no such lord has ever grown great, for the plain arithmetic of the thing defeats them. Command every bloom field in a province and you command the bread of that province, which is to say the smallest part of its eating. The gatherers do not care. The root-finders walk away. A tyrant who starves the countryside into obedience finds after a season that the countryside has simply gone, following the red light over the ridge, and left him his fields and his tax rolls and his hungry soldiers. He has captured the one crop that can be counted, and it is not enough to live on.

title: 6  The Green Bounty
section: 6.4 Of the Markets, and of Those Who Follow the Harvest
text:
6.4 Of the Markets, and of Those Who Follow the Harvest
And yet food must be shared, for no farmer’s fields produce all that a family needeth, and the patchwork of ripening meaneth that there is always surplus somewhere and scarcity somewhere else. The markets of EART-H are therefore not the grand, predictable affairs of a world with regular harvests. They are fluid, shifting gatherings that form and dissolve as the pattern of ripening moveth across the landscape. The market-runners — a class of itinerant traders found in every province — make their living by knowing where the blooms are breaking out and carrying the news from valley to valley, so that surplus may find its way to scarcity before the moment passeth. They travel light and fast, and they are welcomed everywhere, for even the most suspicious community knoweth that without the market-runners, abundance in one place and famine in the next would be the common lot of all.
I have followed these runners on their rounds, and they are among the most knowledgeable people upon EART-H. They carry in their heads a map not of places but of times — where the red surge broke last week, where the thickets will be worth stripping next, which of the few bloom valleys is coming ripe and will pay well for salt. I was told of one runner in Tusque who had not slept in a fixed bed for thirty years and could tell you on any given day which three valleys would yield before the week was out.
What no runner can tell you is where anything will be in a year. That is the whole of it. A world may be fed, and fed well, and still offer no man a rent-roll.
